name: Qualitative Research Methods
summary: Methods for understanding why users behave as they do — their mental models, motivations, frustrations, and language. Small samples, deep data. Best for framing problems, discovering unknowns, and generating hypotheses.

patterns.name: User interviews (semi-structured)
patterns.description: One-on-one conversations guided by an interview script but open to follow-ups. Best for understanding user goals, workflows, decision criteria, and emotional context. Typical length: 30–60 minutes. Sample: 5–8 per user type.
do: Write a discussion guide with ~5–7 open-ended primary questions and 'probes' underneath each
Ask about past behavior: 'Tell me about the last time you [X]' — concrete, memorable, less biased
Use the 5 Whys to chase causation without imposing your own theory
Record (with consent) so you can listen back and quote verbatim
Transcribe or auto-transcribe — otherwise analysis is memory, not data
Run the first 1–2 sessions as pilots; revise the guide based on what didn't land
dont: Ask hypothetical future questions ('would you use this?') — unreliable
Stack multi-part questions — participants only answer the last part
Nod, smile, or react to answers you expected or liked — reinforces acquiescence bias
Show mockups in the first 10 minutes before you understand their context
Interview only 2–3 people and call it a study — n=5+ per user type
patterns.evidence: Nielsen Norman Group's research consistently shows that 5–8 semi-structured interviews per user type surface the dominant themes. Additional interviews yield diminishing returns and should be reserved for edge segments or validation of a specific hypothesis.

patterns.name: Contextual inquiry
patterns.description: Hybrid of interview + observation, conducted in the participant's actual work environment (physical or digital). The researcher watches the user do their real work, asking questions about what they're doing and why. Reveals workarounds, context, and tools invisible in a lab.
do: Ask the user to do the real task with real data — not a scripted scenario
Watch first, ask second — avoid interrupting mid-task
Note down the tools and artifacts they use (other apps, spreadsheets, printouts, sticky notes)
Ask 'why' at natural pause points — not at every click
Use a master-apprentice framing: 'I'm here to learn how you do this'
dont: Bring a long interview script — follow the work, not the script
Ignore 'unrelated' behavior — the workaround often IS the insight
Interrupt mid-flow to ask questions that can wait
Try to train the user on better ways — you're here to observe, not teach
Skip the follow-up synthesis session — the second hour is where patterns emerge
patterns.evidence: Contextual inquiry, originated by Beyer & Holtzblatt (Rapid Contextual Design, 1998), surfaces workarounds, tools, and context that users will not mention in a lab interview — because they don't consciously notice them. Often the most valuable findings for enterprise products come from this method.

patterns.name: Diary studies
patterns.description: Longitudinal self-report method. Participants log behavior, thoughts, or feelings over time (typically 1–4 weeks) via a daily or event-triggered prompt. Good for behavior that happens rarely, is context-dependent, or unfolds over time.
do: Decide cadence: fixed (daily) vs. event-triggered (each time X happens)
Keep entries short — one prompt, 2–3 questions, 2 minutes to complete
Use a tool the participant already has (SMS, WhatsApp, email) — not a new app
Send reminders; expect 50–70% entry completion
Follow up with exit interviews to contextualize patterns you saw in the diary
dont: Require a special app or complex workflow — kills completion
Ask 10 questions per entry — participants drop out
Run without exit interviews — you miss the story behind the data
Forget to incentivize entry completion (daily micro-payment works)
Rely on memory-based questions that defeat the purpose ('what did you do last week?')
patterns.evidence: Diary studies excel at capturing emotion in the moment, rare events, and behavior spread over time (e.g., health, finance, multi-day workflows) — things interviews miss because participants don't remember accurately.

patterns.name: Field studies / ethnographic observation
patterns.description: Researcher embeds in the user's environment for an extended period (hours to days), observing behavior with minimal interference. Best for understanding social context, culture, and tacit knowledge around a product or task.
do: Define what you're looking for (e.g., 'how this workflow moves between people') but stay open to surprises
Take field notes in a structured template — observations, quotes, questions, your interpretations
Spend enough time that the participant stops performing for you (typically a few hours in)
Triangulate with artifacts — photos of their workspace, screenshots, printed forms
dont: Stay only 30 minutes — you'll see the 'show version' of their day
Try to prove a hypothesis — stay in observation mode
Whisper questions constantly — let them work
Generalize from one site — if feasible, visit 2–3
patterns.evidence: Field studies surface the social and cultural context of product use, which laboratory or remote methods cannot. Best used when the product integrates with a physical environment, team workflow, or lived routine.

patterns.name: Intercept studies
patterns.description: Short, opportunistic research with users captured in the moment of product use — via in-app prompt, on-site survey, or in-person approach. Very short (2–5 questions). Good for high-volume, low-depth feedback tied to a specific interaction.
do: Trigger the intercept after a clear completion point — not mid-task
Ask 1–3 questions, focused on what just happened
Mix one closed (scalar) + one open-ended question for richness
Aggregate responses over time; patterns emerge with 100+ responses
Offer a small incentive for longer follow-up interviews when valuable
dont: Interrupt users mid-task — destroys goodwill and data quality
Ask 10 questions — response rate collapses past 3
Use generic NPS — context-free, low-signal
Analyze 10 intercept responses and call it a finding — volume matters
patterns.evidence: Used well, intercept surveys generate large-volume, lightly-structured feedback tied to moments of truth. Best paired with longer qualitative work for the 'why' behind the signal.

checklist: Have you picked a qualitative method whose output will answer your actual question?
Is the sample size appropriate (5–8 for interviews per user type; 10–20 for diary; field: depth over breadth)?
Are your questions open-ended, behavior-focused, and free of leading language?
Is the recruiting screener tight enough to ensure the sample represents your target?
Do you have consent to record, and a plan for secure storage + retention?
Is there a clear decision the study will inform?
Have you planned analysis time equal to at least 2x the data collection time?
